results.result: The 1972 ROSLA policy in the UK mandated an additional year of schooling for individuals born after September 1, 1957, with near 100% compliance. The policy increased formal qualifications, income, and cognition in the general population, though the UK Biobank sample shows only ~10% were affected (vs. 25% in the general population) due to healthy volunteer bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C40, C101-C102 establish ROSLA as a well-documented natural experiment with high compliance and demonstrated behavioral effects. The characterization of the policy, its implementation, and differential impact in UK Biobank vs. general population is supported by multiple citations and data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).

results.result: Using fuzzy local-linear regression discontinuity with MSE-optimized bandwidths (N>30,000, average effective N=5124), the study found no evidence of an effect from an additional year of education on any of six preregistered global neuroimaging measures (total SA, average CT, normalized TBV, mean wFA, WMh, normalized CSF volume; all p's>0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C46 describe the primary causal analysis using appropriate RD methodology with large sample sizes and MSE-optimized bandwidths. The null findings are consistently reported across all global measures with proper statistical testing (p>0.05), supported by Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2. The robustness to missing data imputation strengthens the finding.

results.result: Regional analyses found no effect of an additional year of education on cortical thickness or surface area across 66 cortical regions (average N=5080 and 5392 respectively), weighted mean fractional anisotropy across 27 white matter tracks (mean N=4766), or volume of 18 subcortical regions (mean N=5174), all p'sFDR >0.05.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 extend the null findings to regional analyses with substantial sample sizes and appropriate FDR correction for multiple comparisons. The consistency of null results across multiple brain regions and modalities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) strengthens the overall conclusion of no detectable causal effect.

results.result: Bayesian local randomization analysis comparing participants born in August vs. September 1957 (n≈230) and expanded to a 5-month window (n≈1200) provided strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for all six global neuroimaging measures (BF01 ranging from 11.63 to 18.21 with normal prior mean=0, sd=1), robust across different prior specifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C68 describe a complementary analytical approach that converges with the primary RD analysis. The Bayesian framework provides quantitative evidence for the null hypothesis (BF01>10 for all measures), and sensitivity analyses across different priors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 4 and 6) demonstrate robustness. The expansion to larger windows increases power while maintaining null findings.

results.result: Validation tests confirmed ROSLA as a valid natural experiment: no evidence of manipulation around the cutoff (Tq=-0.72, p=0.47), no associations with placebo outcomes (neuroimaging covariates) except the deterministically related 'summer' variable, consistent across both 1- and 5-month window analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49, C69, C90 establish the internal validity of the natural experiment through standard RD validation procedures. The density test, placebo outcome tests (Supplementary files 1, 5, 7), and consistency with prior literature (Davies et al., 2018; Clark and Royer, 2010, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2018, 2023) provide strong evidence for design validity.

results.result: Correlational analysis in the same participants showed weak to extreme evidence for associations between educational attainment and surface area (BF10=2.3 in 1-month window, BF10=41.7 in 5-month window) and CSF volume (BF10=80.7 in 5-month window), contrasting with null causal findings and demonstrating sensitivity to brain-behavioral associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 demonstrate that the null causal findings are not due to lack of statistical sensitivity, as correlational analyses in the same sample detect associations. This contrast between causal and correlational approaches (Figure 3, Supplementary file 6) is methodologically important and well-supported by the data.

results.result: Post hoc replication across eight additional 10-month cohorts spaced 2 years apart indicated the preregistered associational effect on CSF was likely a false positive, while the association with surface area remained robust across replication cohorts.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 describe important post hoc analyses that test the replicability of the correlational findings. The failure to replicate the CSF association but consistent replication of the SA association (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) provides valuable information about which correlational findings are robust, though this was not preregistered.

results.result: The study finds converging evidence against a causal effect of education on long-term structural neuroimaging outcomes, with null results across imaging modalities (structural MRI, DTI), different regions (cortical, subcortical, white matter), and analysis strategies (continuity-based RD, Bayesian local randomization), while demonstrating sensitivity to detect observational associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C96 synthesize the main findings. The convergence of null results across multiple analytical approaches, brain regions, and imaging modalities, combined with demonstrated sensitivity to correlational effects, provides strong evidence for the absence of detectable long-term causal effects of an additional year of education on brain structure.

results.result: The null neuroimaging findings contrast with established causal effects of education on intelligence, suggesting neural manifestations may be at a resolution not detectable with conventional MRI. The expansion-renormalization theory is proposed as a potential explanation: initial macro-scale changes may have been detectable immediately post-ROSLA but renormalized to micro-scale changes over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C106 present speculative interpretations of the null findings. While the contrast with behavioral effects (C97, supported by citations) is valid, the proposed mechanisms (C98, C103-C106) are speculative and not directly tested. The comparison to short-term intervention studies (C99) raises valid questions but doesn't resolve the discrepancy. Alternative explanations are plausible but unverified.

results.result: The 46-year interval between ROSLA and neuroimaging offers both strengths and weaknesses: while it could allow effects to fade (C108), aging theories predict cumulative protective effects (C109-C110). The design is well-powered to test aging-related 'brain reserve' theories, and findings align with a recent longitudinal study showing education does not affect the rate of brain aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 discuss temporal aspects of the study design. The characterization of strengths/weaknesses is reasonable, but whether 46 years is 'too long' (C108) versus 'particularly well-powered' (C110) for detecting effects remains uncertain. The alignment with Nyberg et al. 2021 (C111) provides some support, but the interpretation depends on untested assumptions about the time course of educational effects on brain structure.

results.result: The study demonstrates that correlational associations between education and brain structure (SA, CSF) do not reflect causal effects, emphasizing the need for caution in attributing causation in non-causal designs. The findings suggest complex pathways and recommend multipronged approaches combining deep phenotyping, longitudinal imaging, and gene-by-environment models.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 draw appropriate methodological conclusions from the contrast between causal and correlational findings. The caution about inferring causation from correlational designs (C113) is well-supported by the data. The recommendations for future research (C118) are reasonable given the findings, though somewhat speculative. The characterization of environmental causes as small and additive (C117) is supported by citations.

results.result: The UK Biobank has healthy volunteer bias with only ~10% affected by ROSLA (vs. 25% in general population), limiting external validity. However, natural experimental design protects against threats to internal validity from selection bias. Results represent a 'local' average treatment effect for UK compliers aged 15-16 in 1973.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C125 appropriately characterize study limitations and the scope of inference. The healthy volunteer bias is well-documented (citations in C70, C119), and the differential impact rate is supported by data (C122-C123, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The discussion of internal vs. external validity tradeoffs (C71, C120, C125) and local average treatment effects (C72, C124) demonstrates appropriate understanding of RD methodology.

results.result: The study reports a lack of causal evidence for long-term neural effects of an additional year of schooling in aging individuals, with findings robust across modalities, regions, and strategies. The results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity and have significant ramifications for theories of aging-related heterogeneity and 'brain reserve'.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77, C126-C127 summarize the main conclusions. The lack of causal evidence is well-supported by the comprehensive null findings. However, the inference that results 'call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity' (C76, C127) is somewhat strong given that the study cannot assess short-term effects and alternative explanations exist (e.g., effects below MRI resolution, expansion-renormalization). The ramifications for aging theories (C77) are appropriately noted but depend on interpretation.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that education is associated with beneficial health, cognitive, and neural outcomes, with correlational evidence across diverse contexts. Brain structure reorganization is proposed as a plausible mechanism, supported by lifespan theories and correlational studies. However, strong causal evidence is lacking due to ethical/practical constraints and complex confounding by sociodemographic, genetic, and selection factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 accurately summarize the state of prior literature and motivation for the study. The characterization of correlational evidence (C1-C10) is well-supported by citations. The identification of the causal inference gap (C11-C16) and confounding issues is appropriate and well-documented. This provides strong justification for the natural experiment approach.

results.result: Natural experiments with regression discontinuity designs allow causal inference in observational phenomena through exogenous assignment mechanisms. Recent econometric advances have standardized RD analysis. Natural experiments have provided robust causal evidence for education's effect on intelligence (0.14-0.35 SD) but have not been applied to cognitive neuroscience questions. The UK Biobank provides an ideal opportunity to test ROSLA's effects on brain structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23, C27 establish the methodological foundation and novelty of the study. The characterization of natural experiments and RD methodology (C17-C21) is accurate and well-cited. The evidence for causal effects on intelligence (C22) provides important context. The claim that natural experiments haven't been used in cognitive neuroscience (C23) represents a knowledge claim that appears accurate. The UK Biobank's suitability (C27) is appropriately documented.

results.result: The availability of large neuroimaging cohorts paired with econometric methods offers new avenues for studying neural effects. Causal inference represents a new tool for neuroimaging with potential to move population neuroscience from association to causation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79, C128 make appropriate forward-looking statements about the methodological contribution. The characterization of causal inference as a 'new tool' for neuroimaging is reasonable given the lack of prior applications (C23). However, the potential to move the field 'from association to causation' is somewhat aspirational and depends on the availability of suitable natural experiments.

results.result: Using a preregistered regression discontinuity design with over 30,000 UK Biobank participants, the study found no evidence that an additional year of education (mandated by the 1972 ROSLA policy) caused changes in any global neuroimaging measures (total surface area, average cortical thickness, normalized total brain volume, mean weighted fractional anisotropy, white matter hyperintensities, or normalized CSF volume). The relationship between year of birth and neural outcomes was continuous around the ROSLA cutoff, and validation tests confirmed ROSLA as a valid natural experiment.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states the analysis 'finds essentially no effect of 1 additional year of secondary education on brain structure in adulthood' and calls it 'convincing' and 'very carefully conducted.' Reviewer 1 notes 'they find essentially no evidence for 1 additional year of education altering brain structure in adulthood' and praises the 'very carefully described and conducted' regression discontinuity analysis. Reviewer 2 confirms the authors 'find no discernible effect of spending an extra year in primary education on brain structure' using 'two complementary, regression-based approaches.'

results.result: Regional analyses found no evidence that an additional year of education caused changes in any of 66 cortical regions for cortical thickness or surface area, 27 white matter fiber tracks for fractional anisotropy, or 18 subcortical regions for volume. These analyses included substantial sample sizes (average N ranging from 4766 to 5392 depending on measure).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these regional null findings as part of the comprehensive analysis. Reviewer 2 specifically notes as a strength that 'the analyses look at both global and local brain measures used as outcomes, thereby assessing a diverse range of brain phenotypes.' The editor and reviewers do not question the regional findings, treating them as consistent with and supporting the main null result.

results.result: As a preregistered robustness test, local randomization analysis in a Bayesian framework was used, comparing participants born in August 1957 to those born in September 1957. This analysis provided strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for all global neuroimaging measures (Bayes Factors ranging from BF01=11.63 to 18.21). Results were robust across different prior specifications and window sizes (1-month and 5-month windows), and placebo outcome tests found no associations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the robustness analyses. Reviewer 1 states 'They completed a large number of diagnostic and alternate analyses to allow for different possible features in the data. (Unlike a positive finding, a negative finding is only bolstered by additional alternative analyses).' Reviewer 2 notes as a strength that 'the authors use multiple methodological approaches, including validation and sensitivity analyses, to investigate the robustness of their findings.' The Bayesian approach is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Correlational analyses (non-causal) in the same sample found evidence for associations between years of education and total surface area (BF10=41.7 in 5-month window) and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF10=80.7), though the CSF association was identified as likely a false positive through post-hoc replication. This contrast between causal and correlational findings demonstrates the difference between the two approaches and provides evidence of sensitivity to brain-behavioral associations in the sample.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these correlational findings as demonstrating methodological sensitivity. Reviewer 2 specifically notes as a strength that the authors 'in the case of correlational analysis, highlight differences with related work by others.' The contrast between null causal findings and positive correlational findings is not questioned, and reviewers treat this as supporting the validity of the null causal result by showing the study had adequate sensitivity to detect associations if they existed.

results.result: The 1972 ROSLA policy raised the minimum mandatory school-leaving age from 15 to 16 in the UK, affecting individuals based on a September 1, 1957 birth date cutoff. Compliance was very high (near 100%), though most adolescents were already continuing past age 15 before the policy. In the UK Biobank sample, approximately 10% of 15-year-olds were estimated to be impacted (compared to 25% in the general UK population), reflecting the healthier, higher SES composition of the UK Biobank. Validation tests found no issues with ROSLA as a natural experiment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the ROSLA policy as a valid natural experiment without raising concerns. Reviewer 2 notes 'other studies have not found specific issues that would invalidate ROSLA as a natural experiment' and describes the approach as 'akin to randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for answering questions of causality.' The editor and reviewers do not question the policy implementation or validation tests.

results.result: The UK Biobank sample has 'healthy volunteer bias' with participants who are healthier, more educated, and of higher SES than the general population. However, natural experimental designs protect against threats to internal validity from selection bias. The study estimates a 'local' average treatment effect for the specific subpopulation (UK, 1973, from 15 to 16 years of age, compliers), offering high internal validity at the expense of external validity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these limitations but do not view them as undermining the findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'the exposure (1 additional year of education) is a very modest manipulation' and that 'a null finding here is completely consistent [with] educational attainment (EA) in fact having an impact on brain structure, where EA may reflect elements of training after second education.' Reviewer 2 states 'This study investigates a well-posed but necessarily narrow question in a specific setting' and notes 'conclusions about the existence or absence of any general effect of the number of years of education on the brain's structure are limited to this specific scenario.' The editor similarly notes 'the impact is limited as the manipulated variable only relates to a single additional year of education.'

results.result: The study reports a lack of causal evidence that a year of school affects long-term neural outcomes in aging individuals. The preregistered findings are robust across imaging modalities, different regions, and analysis strategies. The results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity and have significant ramifications for prominent theories of aging-related heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the main conclusion while noting its scope limitations. The editor calls it 'a valuable finding that adds to the literature on the impact of education on brain health' and states 'the finding is convincing on its own, as the analysis was pre-registered and very carefully conducted.' Reviewer 1 affirms 'the work is of high quality for the precise question asked.' Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'a comprehensive overview of the current state of research in this area' through its discussion. All reviewers accept the null finding as valid within its specific context.

results.result: The null result appears at odds with causal evidence that education increases intelligence, suggesting the neural manifestation may be at a resolution not detectable with conventional MRI. Possible explanations include expansion-renormalization (where cortical changes initially expand then renormalize to a micro-scale over months), the 46-year gap between intervention and imaging, or that effects are detectable only with higher-resolution methods. The timing may actually strengthen tests of aging theories, as education could contribute to both initial brain reserve and cumulative effects over 46 years.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not directly evaluate these speculative interpretations. Reviewer 1 notes 'the outcome measured long after the intervention' and states 'a null finding here is completely consistent [with] educational attainment (EA) in fact having an impact on brain structure' through other mechanisms. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'the modelling approach used in this study requires that all covariates of no interest are equal before and after the cut-off, something that is impossible to test.' The discussion of alternative explanations is noted by Reviewer 2 as providing 'a comprehensive overview' but the specific mechanistic interpretations are neither affirmed nor challenged.

results.result: Natural experiments allow causal inference in observational phenomena through 'random-like' external events outside participants' control. Regression discontinuity (RD) is a widely used causal inference technique applicable when treatment is assigned via a cutoff. Recent econometric advances have optimized and standardized RD analysis. Natural experimental designs have provided robust evidence that education causes intelligence increases (0.14-0.35 SD), but have not previously been used to address questions in cognitive neuroscience.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological framework without question. Reviewer 2 explicitly states that 'Naturalistic experiments of this kind are akin to randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for answering questions of causality.' The editor and reviewers treat the RD methodology as appropriate and well-executed, with Reviewer 1 noting it was 'very carefully described and conducted.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the methodological framework (C17-C23). OpenEval characterizes natural experiments and RD methodology as accurate and well-cited, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm RD as 'akin to randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for answering questions of causality' and note the analysis was 'very carefully described and conducted.'

Both strongly support the Bayesian and robustness analyses (C56-C68). OpenEval notes the Bayesian framework provides quantitative evidence for the null hypothesis with robust sensitivity analyses. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the robustness analyses, noting that 'a negative finding is only bolstered by additional alternative analyses' and commending 'multiple methodological approaches, including validation and sensitivity analyses.'

Both support the characterization of study limitations (C70-C71, C119-C125). OpenEval notes appropriate discussion of healthy volunteer bias, differential impact rates, and internal vs. external validity tradeoffs. Peer reviewers acknowledge these limitations but do not view them as undermining findings, noting the study 'investigates a well-posed but necessarily narrow question in a specific setting' and that 'a null finding here is completely consistent [with] educational attainment having an impact on brain structure' through other mechanisms.

Both support ROSLA as a valid natural experiment (C24-C40, C101-C102). OpenEval characterizes ROSLA as 'well-documented' with 'high compliance and demonstrated behavioral effects.' Peer reviewers accept ROSLA without raising concerns, noting 'other studies have not found specific issues that would invalidate ROSLA as a natural experiment' and describing it as 'akin to randomised controlled trials.'

Both support the main conclusions (C74-C77, C126-C127) while noting scope limitations. OpenEval finds the lack of causal evidence well-supported but notes the inference about 'sustained experience-dependent plasticity' is somewhat strong. Peer reviewers accept the null finding as valid within its specific context, calling it 'convincing' and 'a valuable finding,' while emphasizing that 'conclusions about the existence or absence of any general effect of the number of years of education on the brain's structure are limited to this specific scenario.'

Both support the regional null findings (C50-C55, C93-C95). OpenEval notes the consistency of null results across multiple brain regions with appropriate FDR correction strengthens the overall conclusion. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive analysis, specifically noting as a strength that 'the analyses look at both global and local brain measures used as outcomes, thereby assessing a diverse range of brain phenotypes.'

Both support the correlational analyses demonstrating methodological sensitivity (C80-C87, C112-C113). OpenEval notes the contrast between null causal findings and positive correlational findings is methodologically important. Peer reviewers accept these findings as demonstrating sensitivity, noting as a strength that authors 'in the case of correlational analysis, highlight differences with related work by others' and treating this as supporting the validity of the null causal result.

Both strongly support the primary RD analysis and null findings (C28-C46, C91). OpenEval describes appropriate RD methodology with large sample sizes, MSE-optimized bandwidths, and consistent null results across all global measures. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the finding, with all three reviewers confirming 'essentially no effect of 1 additional year of secondary education on brain structure in adulthood' and calling the analysis 'convincing' and 'very carefully conducted.'

Both rate speculative interpretations as uncertain (C97-C106). OpenEval finds the proposed mechanisms speculative and not directly tested, noting alternative explanations are plausible but unverified. Peer reviewers do not directly evaluate these interpretations but acknowledge 'a null finding here is completely consistent [with] educational attainment having an impact on brain structure' through other mechanisms. Reviewer 2 notes the discussion provides 'a comprehensive overview' but specific mechanistic interpretations are neither affirmed nor challenged.

OpenEval rates temporal aspects as uncertain (C107-C111), questioning whether 46 years is 'too long' versus 'particularly well-powered' for detecting effects. Peer reviewers do not directly evaluate these temporal claims but Reviewer 1 notes 'the outcome measured long after the intervention' and that null findings are consistent with education having impacts through other mechanisms. The temporal interpretation remains unresolved in both evaluations.

OpenEval supports RD validation procedures (C47-C49, C69, C90) including density tests, placebo outcome tests, and consistency with prior literature. Peer reviewers accept the validation without raising concerns, treating ROSLA as a valid natural experiment, though they do not explicitly discuss the specific validation tests mentioned by OpenEval.

OpenEval supports the synthesis of null findings (C88-C96, including C93-C95), noting convergence across multiple analytical approaches provides strong evidence for absence of detectable effects. Peer reviewers accept the comprehensive null findings, with Reviewer 2 specifically noting the strength of analyzing 'both global and local brain measures,' treating the convergence as supporting the main conclusion.

OpenEval supports post hoc replication analyses (C86-C87) testing robustness of correlational findings, noting failure to replicate CSF but consistent SA replication, though not preregistered. Peer reviewers accept correlational findings as demonstrating sensitivity but do not specifically discuss the replication analyses, treating the overall correlational results as supporting the study's methodological validity.

OpenEval supports methodological conclusions about causal vs. correlational inference (C112-C118), noting the caution about inferring causation is well-supported by data.
